findings.text: Global bounce buffer sizing and state queries expose total byte size derived from slab count, early boot adjustment of that count, human readable mapping summary, allocation presence test, and base and limit address queries where the limit reflects either pool end or a growth cap when dynamic expansion remains allowed.

Early boot option parsing consumes a comma separated list where a leading slab quantity is segment aligned, an optional area quantity tunes concurrency sharding, force or noforce keywords control mandatory bouncing versus administrative disable, and a hiwater tracking keyword enables accounting callbacks that are otherwise inert.

Usage accounting maintains a live total with atomic adjustment while the peak value only moves upward through a compare exchange retry that leaves lower totals untouched, teardown paths decrement the total without touching the peak, idle builds use inert handlers, transient pressure and live usage are observable, and peak reset succeeds solely toward the cleared value while other values are rejected.

Early pool creation stays dormant unless an addressing restriction or forced bouncing is present and administrative disable is absent, then it derives sharding from online processor count, repeatedly halves the requested extent on allocation failure until a minimum is reached, materializes slot and area tables, initializes the pool from contiguous firmware memory, registers it globally, and optionally logs the mapping.

Late pool creation and teardown form a paired lifecycle where late setup allocates bounce memory plus management tables from the page allocator with shrinking retries and unwinds partial allocations on failure including special handling for decryption errors that intentionally leaks pages, while teardown reverses encryption state, releases tables and bounce memory through distinct paths for late versus firmware backed pools, and clears the pool descriptor unless forced bouncing pins it.

Dynamic capacity uses background work to append freshly allocated pools within configured size bounds and physical limits with rate limited warnings on failure, while reclamation runs after a grace period to release slot tables and bounce memory before freeing the pool descriptor itself.

Pool membership mutation is serialized by a spin lock held across list insertion and count update, whereas address to pool resolution runs under read side protection without blocking and probes the global collection before per device collections for containment within pool bounds.

Devices default to the shared global bounce state with empty per device collections and bouncing initially disabled where dynamic support exists, attachment to a reserved pool repoints the device toward that pool after first use initializes it, and detachment restores the global default.

Single mapping synchronization enforces direction pairing where device bound work accepts device bound or bidirectional transfers and processor bound work accepts processor bound or bidirectional transfers, with mismatched directions treated as programming errors rather than silent no ops.

Observability nodes are created under a bounce buffer directory exposing slab count and live usage as read only, peak usage as resettable, and transient pressure where dynamic support exists, with creation skipped when no pool exists and with a fully inert variant when debug support is disabled.

Reserved memory integration rejects regions marked reusable or for alternative allocators or unmapped, announces accepted restricted pools, requires linear map accessibility, initializes shared metadata once for first attached device including optional decryption and single shard setup with forced bouncing, and binds later devices to the same state.

Per processor callchain storage centers on a reclaimable container holding a deferred free header followed by a table of processor indexed pointers, where each processor entry bundles room for multiple invocation contexts and each context size reflects base header plus address slots for maximum stack depth and additional context markers.

Callchain buffer lifetime is guarded by a mutex around reference counting where the initial acquirer builds tables and the final releaser clears the global pointer then frees asynchronously, allocation validates requested depth against the global ceiling with distinct errors for corrupt counts versus excessive depth, and release is safe under concurrent puts.

Entry acquisition obtains a per processor recursion slot and fails cleanly when nesting is exhausted or when no buffers are published, otherwise it returns the slot specific region for the current processor, while architecture hooks for kernel and user unwinding default to inert weak definitions and recursion release orders decrement after a barrier.

Failure handling favors containment where decryption failure during attribute update disables the affected pool by marking it fully used, encryption transitions may intentionally leak pages rather than free unsafe memory, high memory attachment and invalid reserved flags are rejected, oversized stack requests are distinguished from internal refcount faults, and unexpected DMA directions trigger fatal checks.

Bounce buffer geometry and control vocabulary are defined by segment size and shift and slab size and default and minimum extents plus area sharding and addressing limit and force control flags and boot keywords for sizing and forcing and hiwater tracking, all interpreted as alignment and bound rules rather than raw numbers here.

Callchain capacity facts comprise global ceilings for stack depth and contexts per stack that bound entry sizing together with a fixed kilobyte scale constant, while debug visibility facts comprise directory and file names for slab count and usage and peak and transient pressure with read only versus resettable permissions.

Callchain services publish acquire and release operations for shared buffers plus per processor entry fetch for recording, alongside overridable kernel and user unwind hooks that do nothing unless architecture code provides them.
